raw_response:
I’m 62 this year, and after 40 years on these 8 mu, I don’t like making big changes just because someone says a new way is better. I have enough schooling to understand the input rates and timing, but in the end I still farm by what has held up on my own land. For Quzhou, wheat-maize is still the safest arrangement for me. Wheat gives steady grain, and maize follows right away, so I keep the land working all year. With only two people in the household, I have to keep the operations simple and timely, especially in the few days between wheat harvest and maize sowing. I have well irrigation, so I won’t gamble on rainfall, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate at the key stages rather than too often. Fertilizer-wise, I’ll stay at a moderate-to-slightly-high level. At my age, I would rather not cut too much and risk the crop turning weak, but I also won’t chase the highest possible yield because this is only 8 mu and every yuan still matters.

For wheat, I’ll use an improved local variety and sow in early October, with base fertilizer at planting and one topdress at jointing. I’ll keep three irrigations in mind: one after sowing if the soil is dry, one at jointing, and one at grain filling if spring stays dry. For maize, I’ll plant immediately after wheat harvest with a hybrid seed, using minimum tillage so I don’t lose time. I’ll put most fertilizer down early and add a topdress around the big flare stage. If summer rain is decent, I may only irrigate once; if it turns dry, I’ll protect the crop at the key stage first. That is how I keep things stable: not too little input, not wasteful input, and no delay in field operations.
